Participants were adults (≥18 years) residing in seven countries: France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Participants from France, Germany, Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States were recruited via Prolific, a widely used crowdsourcing platform for behavioral research, whereas participants from Japan were recruited via Yahoo!
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation, and the study was conducted in accordance with established principles of ethical research conduct.
In addition, choices in the Choice Task were incentivized: participants were informed that they could receive a performance-based bonus with the maximum of £4/¥650 (£0.024/¥5 per correct answer).
For each feature, participants were asked to rank the eight energy sources using a drag-and-drop interface, placing them into boxes labeled from 1 to 8.
During the feedback phase, participants completed a decision-learning task.
Pair order and left-right position were randomized.
In the testing phase, participants completed the same pairwise decision task without feedback.

Additionally, participants completed four self-report questionnaires assessing ecological worldview (NEP), pro-environmental intentions (PEI), scientific literacy (PUS), and social attitudes (SDO), which were not preregistered (Table 1).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Participants are not merely told what is correct, but they experience success and error directly, consolidating knowledge through selfgenerated learning signals.
Participants were adults (≥18 years) residing in seven countries: France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Participants from France, Germany, Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States were recruited via Prolific, a widely used crowdsourcing platform for behavioral research, whereas participants from Japan were recruited via Yahoo!
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation, and the study was conducted in accordance with established principles of ethical research conduct.
In addition, choices in the Choice Task were incentivized: participants were informed that they could receive a performance-based bonus with the maximum of £4/¥650 (£0.024/¥5 per correct answer).
For each feature, participants were asked to rank the eight energy sources using a drag-and-drop interface, placing them into boxes labeled from 1 to 8.
During the feedback phase, participants completed a decision-learning task.
Pair order and left-right position were randomized.
In the testing phase, participants completed the same pairwise decision task without feedback.

Additionally, participants completed four self-report questionnaires assessing ecological worldview (NEP), pro-environmental intentions (PEI), scientific literacy (PUS), and social attitudes (SDO), which were not preregistered (Table 1).
During follow-up, participants completed the societal energy investment preference task first, followed by the belief ranking task.
For both the Belief and Preference Tasks, participants provided ordinal rankings of the eight energy sources.

text.text: Addressing the climate crisis requires citizens to make informed choices about sustainable energy policy, yet public debates are often shaped by inaccurate beliefs about the environmental and health impacts of different energy sources 1,2 .

Misconceptions about key features of energy sources, such as their greenhouse gas emissions, mortality rates, and contribution to electricity production, are particularly dangerous for this debate, as they risk systematically distorting public support for effective decarbonisation strategies 3-5 .
Here we investigate whether a brief reinforcement-based intervention can correct such misconceptions and influence societal investment preferences.

Across seven countries, we reveal systematic misbeliefs, such as overestimating the emissions and mortality of nuclear power and underestimating the mortality of biomass, which were corrected by our intervention across all features and countries.
Furthermore, correcting beliefs led to shifts in preferences towards objectively cleaner and safer energy mixes, and these changes were consistent across countries.
Follow-up assessments indicated that most of our intervention's effects were detectable after 14 weeks.

These results demonstrate a three-step actionable pathway, from behavioural feedback, through belief correction, to preference change, and suggest that short, reinforcement-based interventions could be a scalable tool for improving public decision-making in climate policy and other domains where misconceptions pollute the debate.
Addressing climate change requires coordinated and informed action at multiple levels of decision-making 6 .

text.text: The present study had three aims.
First, to systematically map the structure and magnitude of public misconceptions about key features of major energy sources.
Second, to evaluate whether reinforcement delivered at the level of single behavioural choices can effectively correct beliefs about relational abstract properties of energy sources.

Third, to determine whether belief correction translates into a measurable change in energy preferences, that is, whether belief correction subsequently increases support for cleaner and safer energy options.

To achieve these goals, we conducted a preregistered multi-national experiment involving participants from seven industrialized countries (United Kingdom, United States, France, Italy, Spain, Germany, and Japan; Figure 1A; Table 1).

text.text: We studied misconceptions about three key quantitative indicators: life-cycle CO₂ emissions (including infrastructure and supply chains), mortality rates (deaths from accidents and pollution-related morbidity), and contribution to global electricity production (Figure 1B).

text.text: To conclude, participants' beliefs exhibited specific and robust misconceptions concerning key features of different sources.
To test whether misconceptions at the level of beliefs could be corrected through the reinforcement of simple binary choices, we designed a brief interactive game (Figure 1D).
text.formatted: To test whether misconceptions at the level of beliefs could be corrected through the reinforcement of simple binary choices, we designed a brief interactive game (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1D</ref>).

text.text: The intervention leveraged pairwise comparisons between energy sources, because what ultimately matters is the relative rank of energy sources within each feature, and binary comparisons can in principle modify the overall rank.

On each trial, participants were presented with a pair of energy sources and asked to identify, depending on the feature being evaluated, which one had the least CO₂ emissions, induced the least deaths or produced the most electricity worldwide.
They immediately received binary feedback (winning or losing an incentivized point), indicating correct and incorrect responses respectively.
Each feature (CO₂, death, production) was trained in independent 2.5-minute blocks (24 trials in total).

The design deliberately mirrored key ingredients of efficient reinforcement learning: participants actively committed to choices (agency), received immediate and unambiguous feedback, and operated within a simplified binary structure that minimized cognitive load 18, 23, 24 .
text.formatted: The design deliberately mirrored key ingredients of efficient reinforcement learning: participants actively committed to choices (agency), received immediate and unambiguous feedback, and operated within a simplified binary structure that minimized cognitive load <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref> .

text.text: Following the feedback phase, participants performed a testing phase in which the same pairwise comparisons were presented again without feedback: correct choices were still incentivized during this phase, but no feedback was provided, with this step aimed at promoting knowledge consolidation rather than continued learning.

As expected, choice accuracy in the reinforcement learning task improved rapidly across the learning phase and remained significantly higher than baseline during the feedback-free testing phase, for all three features (Figure 3A and Supplementary Figure 2).

text.text: To assess whether learning transferred from simple reinforced binary choices to abstract relational knowledge (the "cognitive map" of the energy sources within each feature) participants repeated the original dragand-drop belief task after the RL intervention (Figure 1F).

We used a GLMM (M2) predicting correctness from the same Phase predictor, the population-level misconception (i.e., average baseline inaccuracy), and their interaction.

text.text: In conclusion, our brief RL-based intervention effectively corrected misconceptions about key features of energy sources.

In conclusion, our delayed assessments indicated that, although the effects were somewhat reduced, both belief corrections and preference changes remained statistically detectable (at the meta-analytical level, and in most countries) up to twelve weeks after the intervention.
Our preregistered multi-national study demonstrates that large and systematic misconceptions about energy sources exist across industrialized countries.

Importantly, these misconceptions can be efficiently corrected through a brief behavioural intervention based on the reinforcement of simple binary choices, and that belief correction translates into more environmentally rational energy preferences.
Our findings replicated across seven samples that varied in country of origin, demographic profile, and attitudinal make-up strengthening our confidence in their robustness 27.

text.text: The pattern of misbeliefs we observed is instructive.

The persistent overestimation of oil's role likely stems from its visibility in transport and domestic use, conflating general fuel consumption with electricity production 28 -a distortion further amplified by availability heuristics: oil is so omnipresent in people's daily lives and media environment that its perceived importance is systematically inflated beyond its actual contribution to electricity generation.

text.text: The favorable view of biomass may reflect a "naturalness bias," whereby processes associated with organic matter are automatically judged as benign 29 .

text.text: Most strikingly, the misconception surrounding nuclear energy (perceived as both unsafe and highly polluting) reveals the deep imprint of cultural and historical associations.
Nuclear power has been symbolically linked with weapons and catastrophe, a connection reinforced by media coverage of accidents such as Chernobyl and Fukushima 30, 31 .

text.text: However, when assessed using quantitative indicators such as lifecycle CO₂ emissions and mortality rates, nuclear energy is often found to rank among the safest and lowest-carbon large-scale energy sources.

These findings underscore the broader challenge of aligning public beliefs with empirical evidence across the entire energy landscape, emphasizing the need for evidence-based educational strategies to foster informed decision-making.

While previous behavioural intervention studies have overlooked this dimension [32] [33] [34] , our results suggest that reinforcement learning offers a promising cognitive framework for such interventions 35 .

text.text: In contrast to traditional nudges or passive information campaigns (such as factsheets, instructional videos, or educational materials that deliver knowledge without requiring active engagement), RL-based training engages active par-ticipation, immediate feedback, and intrinsic motivation through small rewards.
Participants are not merely told what is correct, but they experience success and error directly, consolidating knowledge through selfgenerated learning signals.
Critically, this process unfolds across three distinct levels.
At the most atomic level, reinforcement operates on single binary choices, shaping behavioural accuracy through trial-and-error feedback.
These repeated local corrections then aggregate into an updated relational representation of how energy sources compare across key features 36, 37 .
text.formatted: These repeated local corrections then aggregate into an updated relational representation of how energy sources compare across key features <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">37</ref> .

text.text: Finally, it is this restructured belief system, rather than any direct persuasion, that drives the observed shifts in energy preferences.

The robustness of this chain across features, countries and time suggests that reinforcementbased learning does not merely produce transient performance gains, but genuinely reorganises the mental models that underpin decision-making.

As such, our results suggest that reinforcementbased interventions for belief change deserve a more prominent place in the growing literature on the application of cognitive models to behavioural public policy 23, 35, [38] [39] [40] .

text.text: In line with previous studies 41 , we hypothesize that the success of reinforcement-based interventions depends on a set of general principles: agency enhances retention 42, 43 ; immediate feedback accelerates learning 44, 45 ; and binary choices and outcome information simplifies complex domains 24, 46 .

text.text: Translating these principles into impactful tools requires balancing engagement and scalability.
While our 15-minute intervention already compares favorably with many educational modules, further streamlining is feasible.

Adaptive algorithms could target feedback selectively to the misconceptions most in need of correction, or focus on the most influential dimensions (CO₂ and mortality rates), which are themselves strongly correlated.
Several limitations of our study delineate directions for future work.
First, our sample was restricted to seven highly industrialized nations.

These were selected to encompass diverse historical and policy attitudes toward energy (each having implemented a nuclear program and facing choices about future decarbonization), but do not represent the full global spectrum.
Extending this approach to emerging economies, where energy transitions will have the largest marginal impact, is an essential next step.
Second, our intervention addressed only three dimensions of energy evaluation.

While CO₂ emissions and mortality rates capture the ethical and environmental axes of decision-making, real policy preferences also depend on economic and geopolitical considerations, notably the financial cost of implementing a given energy source, the availability of the required materials (including rare earths and uranium), and the lead time from planning to actual deployment.
Integrating these additional factors would allow testing whether cognitive correction in one domain generalizes or competes with others.
Third, although our delayed assessments indicate encouraging persistence, the fact that delay was confounded with the country factor in our samples prevented a proper assessment of the time course.
Controlled longitudinal designs could clarify the temporal dynamics of these effects and identify ways to strengthen their persistence.
Finally, reinforcement-based interventions, unlike simple informational nudges, require an engaged and attentive audience.
This constraint limits immediate scalability but also opens opportunities for integration into educational systems or digital learning platforms.
Online courses, interactive modules, or gamified climateeducation apps could easily embed similar feedback structures at negligible marginal cost.
The intrinsic appeal of game-like reinforcement dynamics may further enhance voluntary participation and knowledge retention.
Taken together, our results highlight both the scale of public misconceptions about energy and the cognitive potential of reinforcement learning to address them.
In a policy landscape often polarized between technocratic expertise and public skepticism, fostering informed agency through active learning could represent a missing link.

By enabling individuals to reconstruct accurate mental models of the energy landscape, reinforcementbased approaches can help bridge the gap between scientific consensus and democratic decision-making: an essential step toward collective climate rationality.

The study was conducted across seven countries (France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States).
Study materials were translated into the official languages of the country using a forward-backward translation procedure.

The experiment comprised three tasks: a belief ranking task, a reinforcement-based intervention task, and a societal energy investment preference ranking task.
Both the preference and belief ranking tasks were administered before (pre-intervention) and after (post-intervention) the intervention.
In the pre-intervention phase, the preference ranking task always preceded the belief ranking task, whereas in the post-intervention phase, it followed the belief ranking task.

The belief ranking task aimed to assess participants' beliefs about how eight energy sources compare across three features: (1) life-cycle CO₂ emissions (including infrastructure and supply chains), (2) mortality rates, defined as deaths due to accidents and pollution-related morbidity, and (3) contribution to global electricity production.
For each feature, participants were asked to rank the eight energy sources using a drag-and-drop interface, placing them into boxes labeled from 1 to 8.

Rankings were feature-specific: for life-cycle CO₂ emissions, 1 corresponded to the lowest emissions and 8 to the highest; for mortality rates, 1 indicated the lowest number of deaths and 8 the highest; and for electricity production, 1 indicated the highest contribution and 8 the lowest (Supplementary Instructions).
Participants could freely reorder the energy sources before confirming their response.
The order of presentation of the three features was randomized across participants.
The reinforcement-based intervention consisted of two phases (a feedback phase and a testing phase).
For each feature, the two phases were presented consecutively in blocks, with the order of feature blocks randomized across participants.
The incentive structure was explicitly described in the task instructions.
Participants received a bonus of £0.024 (or ¥5 for Japanese samples) per correct response, with a maximum of £2.016 (¥420) per phase and feature under perfect performance.
During the feedback phase, participants completed a decision-learning task.

For each feature, they were presented with all 28 possible pairwise combinations of the eight energy sources and selected the option they believed had the lowest CO 2 emissions, the fewest deaths, or the highest electricity production, respectively (Supplementary Instructions).

Following each choice, the selected option was highlighted by a colored border for 500 ms, after which explicit feedback indicating the correct answer was presented for 1,500 ms using a frame and an arrow.
An Inter-Trial Interval (ITI) of 200 ms preceded the next trial.
Pair order and left-right position were randomized.
In the testing phase, participants completed the same pairwise decision task without feedback.
All pairwise combinations were presented again for each feature, and participants made a choice for each pair.
The same timing parameters were used for choice confirmation, ITI and randomization, but no feedback was provided.
The societal energy investment preference task assessed participants' preferences regarding public investment in energy sources.

At both the beginning and the end of the experiment, participants ranked the eight energy sources according to the level of societal investment they considered appropriate (Supplementary Instructions).
This ranking served as an index of policy preference.
Instructions prompted participants to indicate which energy sources they believed were most worthwhile to invest in.

The eight energy sources were displayed in a randomized order, and participants ranked them by dragging and dropping each source into boxes labelled from 1 to 8, from highest to lowest investment priority.
Participants could revise their rankings freely before confirming their response.

Additionally, participants completed four self-report questionnaires assessing ecological worldview (NEP), pro-environmental intentions (PEI), scientific literacy (PUS), and social attitudes (SDO), which were not preregistered (Table 1).

For both the Belief and Preference Tasks, participants provided ordinal rankings of the eight energy sources.
From these rankings, we inferred the full set of implied pairwise choices between all possible energy pairs, yielding a binary choice outcome for each pair.
For the Belief Task, we compared simulated choices to empirical ground-truth rankings (Our World in Data) to infer choice correctness (1 = correct,0 = incorrect) for each pairwise comparison.
These inferred binary outcomes constituted the dependent variable in the beliefaccuracy models.
For the Preference Task, no objective correctness criterion exists.

Instead, we computed preference dissimilarity as a binary indicator of whether a participant's implied choice for a given energy pair changed between pre-and post-feedback (or between pre-feedback and delay;0 = same choice,1 = different choice).
This measure indexed preference change.
Above transformations were pre-registered.
All models and tests were estimated separately for each country (see Supplementary Materials 3).
To derive population-level estimates which we report in the text, we conducted random-effects meta-analyses using country-level statistics and standard errors.
Random-effects models were chosen to account for expected heterogeneity across national samples.
Between-country variance was estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

For regression models, meta-analyses were based on country-level regression results (estimate and standard error) and were implemented in R (v4.4.2) using the rma() function (method = "REML") from the metafor package (v4.8-0).
For the descriptive tests, meta-analyses were conducted using country-level means (accuracy or discrepancy) and variances.
They were implemented in Python (v3.11.13) using the meta_regression() function (method = "reml") of the pymare package (v0.0.10).
All meta-analytical results are reported using the following format : effect size (β), standard errors (SE), zstatistics (z), p-values (p), 95% confidence intervals (CI).
Country-level estimation and meta-analytic aggregation were pre-registered.
In addition to regression models, we conducted descriptive tests: 1) on baseline accuracy level of participants' beliefs and 2) on baseline discrepancy between energy sources.
Both descriptive tests, country-level and metaanalytic, were implemented in Python (v3.11.13).
The first descriptive test assesses whether baseline belief accuracy (across features, in %) exceeds chance level of 50%.
We thus performed by country a onesample t-test, two-sided, against 50.
This test was implemented using the ttest_1samp function from the scipy.stats module (scipy v1.11.4).
The reported metaanalytical results use the mean and variance of countrylevel accuracy.

The second descriptive test assesses whether baseline discrepancy (difference between the empirical rank in the belief task and its actual rank) of energy sources are statistically different between one another (across features).
We thus performed by country a two related sample t-test, two-sided, of the discrepancy levels of pairs of energy sources.
This test was implemented using the ttest_rel function from the scipy.stats module (scipy v1.11.4).
The reported meta-analytical results use the mean and variance of country-level discrepancy differences.
The full meta-analytical and country-level statistical results of both tests are described in Main Supplemen-tary Materials and Supplementary Materials 3 respectively.
All country-level regression models and their metaanalytic aggregation were implemented in R (v4.4.2).

Generalized linear mixed-effects models (Models M1, M2, M4 and M6) were estimated using the glmer() function from the lme4 package (v1.1-37), with a binomial family (logit link), the bobyqa optimizer, and control settings optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5).
Cumulative link models (Models M3, M5 and M7) were estimated using the clmm() function, with adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature (nAGQ = 20), from the ordinal package (v2023.12-4.1).

When testing effects not directly estimated by the model, linear contrasts were constructed by specifying contrast vectors over the fixed-effect coefficients (including main effects and interaction terms) and evaluated using the model's t_test() method in Python (v3.11.13).
